Sacred Traces

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A forensic artist is using foraged materials to recreate the paints and brushes used by San people thousands of years ago.

Unique Selling Point:
Stephen Townley Bassett has dedicated his life to the study and recreation of rock art. He is a forensic artist living in the town Komani in the Eastern Cape and has spent decades experimenting with pigments, using foraged materials to recreate the paints and brushes used by San rock artists. As a young man, studying archaeology at the University of Stellenbosch, he spent almost two years documenting San rock art sites in the Cederberg.





Summary:
Stephen uses technology to help reproduce paintings that have faded over time. He does not use ordinary paints, but instead has experimented for years using bones, eggshells and the faeces of raptors to create pigments. He also makes his brushes, even using the hair of a ground squirrel once. He tries to get into the headspace of the artists whose work he recreates.

He was inspired by his uncle’s interest in rock art and remembers seeing his first San painting at the age of 14. His uncle Ginger Townley Johnson also documented hundreds of rock art sites across South Africa. Stephen believes these paintings were a portal to another dimension, a spirt world that existed on the other side of the rock.



Further information:
Dr Siyakha Mguni, who is a professor at UCT’s Michaelis Art school in Cape Town will also talk to us. He teaches rock art to students and has studied towards understanding and preserving southern Africa’s ancient visual arts heritage for the past thirty years.

Script:


NATSOUND: I’ve got some water from the river here. I’m just going to cool it down.

VO 1 In the Stormberg mountains …

VO 2 The gallbladder of a Springbok, ochre, and bone marrow fat - ancient ingredients - are being transformed into pigments of the past.

NATSOUND

VO 3 With fire, stone and earth - techniques used to create San rock art - are brought to life.

NATSOUND You’re going to see magic in that yellow pigment that you see in front of you is going to change into an orangey red colour and that would have expanded the palette of the San artist.

VO 4 One of the oldest cultures in the world, indigenous to southern Africa, the San are hunter-gatherers known for their deep knowledge of nature …. and intricate rock paintings. (use getty visuals / videos of the San)

UPSOUND Stephen Townley Bassett: It’s the earliest art form that we have in Southern Africa. In caves and rocky outcrops,, there’s a huge gallery, an outdoor gallery, that also needs to be appreciated and looked after.

UPSOUND Dr Siyakha Mguni / Archaeologist: The oldest evidence that we have is plus minus 30 000 years ago which is a site called appollo 11 in the southern part of Namibia just across the border from South Africa.

VO 5 Dr Siyakha Mguni is an archaeologist who teaches rock art at UCT’s Michaelis School of Fine Art. (Day 1 at Michaelis)

VO 6 He says it ended when the region was colonised, but what remains at rock art sites across the country is a window into the world of the people who made it.

UPSOUND Dr Siyakha Mguni: The story we can glean from the rock art is diverse and vast. There’s talk of you know the trance dances having been the most important ritual. This art is a reflection of humanity. At it’s core.

VO 7 He says the art is sophisticated, and shows the ability to think creatively dates back thousands of years.

UPSOUND Dr Siyakha Mguni: Once you learn the code you can peel off the different layers of meaning.

VO 8 For decades, forensic artist Stephen Townley Bassett has been trying to crack that code. He’s spent years experimenting with making brushes and paints he believes the San would have used - to create what he calls documentary paintings.

VO 9 In a suburb of Komani, a town situated in the heart of the Eastern Cape, he has been quietly, obsessively, single mindedly recreating the ancient art traditions of the San in his studio.

NATSOUND Erin: What a space.
NATSOUND Stephen: This is my man cave and some of the tools of my trade.

UPSOUND Stephen: My life has really been about the how? How do they make their brushes, how did they make their paint, how can we still see these paintings on the rock thousands of years later?

VO 10 The Cederberg mountains in the Western Cape is where some of the most well preserved San rock art can be found - and it’s where Stephen first discovered it.

UPSOUND: Stephen: And I think I saw my first painting in the Citrusdal area when I was about fourteen.

VO 11 The fascination for rock art runs in his family - his grandfather, Frederick, would search for rock art in the early 1900s.

UPSOUND Stephen Townley Bassett / Forensic Artist: One’s childhood plays actually a very big part in one’s life later on. In my case, it did. My father died suddenly of a heart attack when I was four years old.

VO 12 Stephen’s uncle, Richard Townley Johnson, became a father figure - affectionately known as Ginger because of his red hair, he was renowned for documenting San rock art.

UPSOUND Stephen Townley Bassett / Forensic Artist: I was just too happy to be out with him, and he was a very adventurous character. And he would take me to sites and I’d carry his bag, or his camera, tracing film, whatever it was, food.

VO 13 And now, he too documents and recreates rock art. But, Stephen’s days are not always spent in his studio - often he’ll spend weeks in the field. This time, I get to join… for a day.

LINK: We’re on our way to a secret location, a rock art site on privately owned land, behind locked gates.

VO 14 About an hour away from Komani, is a rock shelter that offers a glimpse into the lives of the San.

VO 15 And because it’s not accessible to the public - it’s protected from a more sinister threat to its preservation.

UPSOUND Stephen: Graffiti begets more grafitti. So, at public sites, its’ important that graffiti is taken off as soon as possible. It’s disturbing and its disconcerting. And I think that’s what got me on a road in terms of conservation, rehabilitating sites.

VO 16 And it’s why documenting and reproducing rock art - to conserve it for future generations - has become his life’s work.

UPSOUND Stephen Townley Bassett: I think the art is very closely integrated with their belief systems and their spirituality. So, I always say to people when you go to a cave, behave as you would in a place of worship. Be respectful of what you are seeing on the rockface.

Stephen: Paintings are up to the right here.
Erin: Gosh
Stephen: These will be hundreds and some thousands of years old.
Erin: Gosh. It just keeps going.
Stephen: Then you’ve got these large bodies that you see here are the bodies of eland. Here’s a whole panel of Eland here.
Erin: Jeepers. Look at that.
Stephen: Can you imagine what this looked like when it was still fresh?

VO 17 The eland was believed to have supernatural powers. It was more than just a food source - it was a sacred being linked to the spiritual world.

UPSOUND Stephen Townley Bassett: What interests me is here in the middle, you’ve got an eland that’s been painted in red, behind it and above it is in yellow. I sometimes wonder why, it’s essentially a spiritual art, a religious art, why certain eland were painted in certain colours.

VO 18 It’s fat and blood were used to make pigments for painting.

UPSOUND Dr Siyakha Mguni: It was an animal that was believed to be powerful, to be potent. So when you grab that material, that is the container of that potency, so you’re taking that potency and imbuing it with something that’s powerful. So you’ve created or recreated that power in the image.

LINK: Stephen has been experimenting with paint and brushes for decades using materials like feathers, porcupine quills, reeds. He tries to recreate the ancient processes used thousands of years ago.

VO 19 Analysing the art, trying to figure out just how it was created, takes time and patience - it’s called experimental archaeology and Stephen is obsessive about the detail.

UPSOUND Stephen Townley Bassett: What intrigued me was the way the paint has been applied to the surface of the rock.
Erin: It’s so detailed, what do you notice?
Stephen: If you look closely here, there are very fine whiskers on this lion. Now, what kind of implement would have been used to draw out those whiskers?
And I believe it would have been instruments that I have in my hand here. That I’ve made myself. Over the years I’ve done many tests and many trials and I would say whiskers like that would have been done with the tip of a feather.

VO 20 Making the paints has also taken years of experimenting.

NATSOUND
Erin: Can I try?
Stephen: Yes, absolutely.

UPSOUND Dr Siyakha Mguni: Sourcing the pigments, working with the pigments, all the way up to the end product, that in itself is is is a trail that can to some degree lead you from the natural into a different space.

LINK: What if a painting could unlock another dimension? Rock art is far more than decoration. It’s believed it was a spiritual gateway and now Stephen is using technology to peel back the layers.

VO 21 Stephen is able to include in his reproductions parts of paintings that have faded over time.

UPSOUND Stephen Townley Bassett: Certainly the camera equipment I’ve got today is much better than my uncle had. And the recording techniques. Although it gives you false colour, it will show me that what I can barely see with the naked eye on the rock face, suddenly putting it through the software, there’s an eland. And that for me is fascinating.

VO 22 And accuracy, using the paints and brushes that would have been used, is a crucial part of the process.

UPSOUND Stephen Townley: So when they look at a documentary painting of mine, A they will see more than what they can see on the rock face at the site, and B they will be seeing pigments that have come from the African soil.

VO 23 Stephen’s life pursuit has been one of blood, sweat and tears.

UPSOUND Erin: What’s this? Is this real blood over here?
USOUND Stephen: It is, it is. This is actually my blood. I have got also lion blood and various animals, you know the blood of those animals that I keep and I use in the paint making process.

UPSOUND Stephen Townley Bassett: Some of these caves are very difficult to get to, or take a lot of sweat to get to them, and then using my own blood, and there are tears sometimes, when I can’t find the cave I’m looking for and I have to go home empty handed.

VO 24 Stephen plans to continue his uncle Ginger’s work by documenting an art form that is continuously being eroded - by bringing it to the public, with an exhibition of his reproductions in the next year.
